Proof by Contrapositive

Lay out an even-odd table and set a statement beside its contrapositive. This is the detour for when the direct road is blocked.

Some statements resist a frontal attack. Then flip and negate: prove the contrapositive instead. It always shares the original's truth value. Settle one side and the other comes free.

For example, if a square is even, the number itself is even. Instead of studying squares, look only at odd numbers. Squaring an odd number always gives an odd number. So an even square never came from an odd number.

n2 even⇒n even  ⟺  n odd⇒n2 oddn^2 \text{ even} \Rightarrow n \text{ even} \iff n \text{ odd} \Rightarrow n^2 \text{ odd}n2 even⇒n even⟺n odd⇒n2 odd
(2k+1)2=2(2k2+2k)+1(2k+1)^2 = 2(2k^2+2k)+1(2k+1)2=2(2k2+2k)+1

Examples & Exercises

Prove completely, by contrapositive, that for an integer nnn, "if n2n^2n2 is even then nnn is even".

Reduce the claim to its contrapositive, "if nnn is odd then n2n^2n2 is odd", and prove that by the odd-square expansion.

n2 even⇒n even⟺n odd⇒n2 oddn^2 \text{ even} \Rightarrow n \text{ even} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n \text{ odd} \Rightarrow n^2 \text{ odd}n2 even⇒n even⟺n odd⇒n2 odd
Show proof

  1. The claim is P⇒QP \Rightarrow QP⇒Q with PPP: "n2n^2n2 is even" and QQQ: "nnn is even". An implication is logically equivalent to its contrapositive (both fail exactly when PPP is true and QQQ false), so we prove ¬Q⇒¬P\lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P¬Q⇒¬P: "if nnn is odd then n2n^2n2 is odd".

  2. The contrapositive is proved directly: if nnn is odd, then n=2k+1n = 2k + 1n=2k+1 for some integer kkk, and n2=(2k+1)2=4k2+4k+1=2(2k2+2k)+1n^2 = (2k+1)^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1n2=(2k+1)2=4k2+4k+1=2(2k2+2k)+1.

    Since 2k2+2k2k^2 + 2k2k2+2k is an integer, n2n^2n2 is odd.

    Check in the scene: n=7n = 7n=7 gives k=3k = 3k=3 and n2=49=2⋅(2⋅9+6)+1=2⋅24+1n^2 = 49 = 2 \cdot (2 \cdot 9 + 6) + 1 = 2 \cdot 24 + 1n2=49=2⋅(2⋅9+6)+1=2⋅24+1.

    The contrapositive is proved, so by equivalence the original claim "if n2n^2n2 is even then nnn is even" is proved.

    (Why the direct attempt stalls: the assumption n2=2mn^2 = 2mn2=2m gives no handle for computing with nnn — the contrapositive swaps it for the workable form n=2k+1n = 2k + 1n=2k+1.)

    (2k+1)2=4k2+4k+1=2(2k2+2k)+1(2k+1)^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 2(2k^2 + 2k) + 1(2k+1)2=4k2+4k+1=2(2k2+2k)+1

Prove by contrapositive that for an integer nnn, "if 3n+23n + 23n+2 is odd then nnn is odd".

First explain why the direct route is awkward: "3n+23n + 23n+2 odd" only yields "3n3n3n odd", with no direct grip on nnn itself.

3n+2 odd⇒n odd⟺n even⇒3n+2 even3n + 2 \text{ odd} \Rightarrow n \text{ odd} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n \text{ even} \Rightarrow 3n + 2 \text{ even}3n+2 odd⇒n odd⟺n even⇒3n+2 even
Show proof

  1. Why the direct route is awkward: assuming 3n+23n + 23n+2 is odd gives 3n=(3n+2)−23n = (3n + 2) - 23n=(3n+2)−2, so 3n3n3n is odd.

    But passing from "3 times nnn is odd" to "nnn is odd" needs a separate argument that nnn cannot be even — there is no computable form of nnn to work with.

    So we turn to the contrapositive: "if nnn is even then 3n+23n + 23n+2 is even".

  2. Prove the contrapositive directly: if nnn is even, write n=2kn = 2kn=2k with kkk an integer; then 3n+2=3(2k)+2=6k+2=2(3k+1)3n + 2 = 3(2k) + 2 = 6k + 2 = 2(3k + 1)3n+2=3(2k)+2=6k+2=2(3k+1).

    Since 3k+13k + 13k+1 is an integer, 3n+23n + 23n+2 is even.

    The contrapositive is proved, so by equivalence the original claim "if 3n+23n + 23n+2 is odd then nnn is odd" is proved.

    Check in the scene: n=8=2⋅4n = 8 = 2 \cdot 4n=8=2⋅4 gives 3n+2=26=2(3⋅4+1)=2⋅133n + 2 = 26 = 2(3 \cdot 4 + 1) = 2 \cdot 133n+2=26=2(3⋅4+1)=2⋅13, even.

Prove that for an integer nnn, "if n2n^2n2 is divisible by 3 then nnn is divisible by 3".

Take the contrapositive, then split the case "3 does not divide nnn" into n=3k+1n = 3k + 1n=3k+1 and n=3k+2n = 3k + 2n=3k+2, showing in each case that 3 does not divide n2n^2n2.

n=3k+1⇒n2=3(3k2+2k)+1,n=3k+2⇒n2=3(3k2+4k+1)+1n = 3k+1 \Rightarrow n^2 = 3(3k^2 + 2k) + 1, \qquad n = 3k+2 \Rightarrow n^2 = 3(3k^2 + 4k + 1) + 1n=3k+1⇒n2=3(3k2+2k)+1,n=3k+2⇒n2=3(3k2+4k+1)+1
Show proof

  1. We prove the contrapositive: "if 3 does not divide nnn then 3 does not divide n2n^2n2".

    By the division algorithm, if 3 does not divide nnn the remainder is 1 or 2, so n=3k+1n = 3k + 1n=3k+1 or n=3k+2n = 3k + 2n=3k+2 for some integer kkk.

    Compute each case.

  2. Case 1: if n=3k+1n = 3k + 1n=3k+1 then n2=9k2+6k+1=3(3k2+2k)+1n^2 = 9k^2 + 6k + 1 = 3(3k^2 + 2k) + 1n2=9k2+6k+1=3(3k2+2k)+1 — remainder 1 on division by 3, so 3 does not divide n2n^2n2.

    Case 2: if n=3k+2n = 3k + 2n=3k+2 then n2=9k2+12k+4=3(3k2+4k+1)+1n^2 = 9k^2 + 12k + 4 = 3(3k^2 + 4k + 1) + 1n2=9k2+12k+4=3(3k2+4k+1)+1 — again remainder 1, so 3 does not divide n2n^2n2.

    Both cases give the contrapositive's conclusion, so the contrapositive is proved, and by equivalence so is the original claim.

    Check in the scene: n=9=3⋅3n = 9 = 3 \cdot 3n=9=3⋅3 is divisible by 3 and n2=81=3⋅27n^2 = 81 = 3 \cdot 27n2=81=3⋅27 is too.
